question: Why did the Fifth Circuit panel in Hamilton v. Dallas County affirm dismissal even though it said the County's gender-based weekend scheduling policy appeared to violate Title VII?
reference_notes: Must mention: circuit precedent limits adverse employment actions to ultimate employment decisions such as hiring, firing, promoting or compensating; the rule of orderliness binds the panel; denial of full weekends off is not an ultimate employment decision.
cited_authority: Welsh v. Fort Bend Indep. Sch. Dist., 941 F.3d 818, 824 (5th Cir. 2019)
rater_a_reason: cl7797513:5 states the ultimate-employment-decision requirement and cl7797513:6 completes the point and concludes the denial of weekends off is not such a decision.

claim: The Fifth Circuit rejected Ayorinde's retaliation claim only for lack of a causal link, accepting that he engaged in protected activity when he asked for his test to be uploaded.
label: unsupported_claim
cited_authority: Davenport v. Edward D. Jones & Co., L.P., 891 F.3d 162, 167 (5th Cir. 2018)
rater_a_reason: Step 4: cl10737190:6 says Ayorinde 'fails to identify any evidence suggesting that he participated in a protected activity or that his supervisor consequently retaliated'; no passage says protected activity was accepted.
construction_note: Started from supported claim (no evidence of protected activity or retaliation); changed to say protected activity was accepted and only causation failed (misattributes the basis of the holding).

claim: Taking the allegations as true, the Fifth Circuit panel treated the sergeant's statement that the scheduling policy was based on gender as direct evidence of discrimination because no inference is needed to reach the discriminatory motive.
label: supported
cited_authority: Portis v. First Nat’l Bank of New Albany, 34 F.3d 325, 329 (5th Cir. 1994)
rater_a_reason: Step 1: cl7797513:4 says plaintiffs alleged direct evidence because the sergeant's statement 'shows a discriminatory motive on its face' and 'no inference or presumption is required'.

claim: The McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting test does not apply where the plaintiff presents direct evidence of discrimination, in which case the employer must show it would have made the same decision regardless of the forbidden factor.
label: right_doc_wrong_passage
rater_a_reason: Step 2: cl7797513:3 quotes Thurston that 'the McDonnell Douglas test is inapplicable where the plaintiff presents direct evidence' and says the burden then shifts to the employer on the same-decision showing; cited cl7797513:2 only says discrimination may be proved by direct or circumstantial evidence.
construction_note: Claim paraphrases Hamilton chunk 3; cited chunk 2 is the preceding passage on proof methods in the same opinion.

claim: An employer can defeat an FMLA claim even if it was mistaken, because a supervisor's ignorance of why the employee took leave and her unsupported assumptions do not show she lacked a genuine belief that the employee was abusing leave.
label: supported
rater_a_reason: Step 1: cl11118835:20 says Warren's assumptions were mistaken but her ignorance and unsupported assumptions 'does not suggest that she did not really believe' Paterakos was abusing leave.

claim: To make out a prima facie retaliation case on circumstantial evidence, a plaintiff must show protected activity, an adverse employment action, and a causal connection between the two.
label: wrong_document
cited_authority: Vichio v. US Foods, Inc., 88 F.4th 687, 691 (7th Cir. 2023)
rater_a_reason: Step 3: cl10737190:5 (Ayorinde, different opinion) states the three prima facie retaliation elements; cited cl11118835:12 concerns proving pretext in a discrimination case.
construction_note: Claim paraphrases Ayorinde chunk 5; cited chunk is Paterakos chunk 12 on pretext.
